A1.justification: Both PDFs describe VideoHallu and retain its 3,233-pair synthetic-video dataset. The main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and can be matched despite substantial restructuring.

before.justification: v3 reports original model evaluations and curriculum-based fine-tuning experiments in Section 3 and Tables 2–3, with additional analyses and cases in the appendices.

after.justification: v4 reports original benchmark evaluations, SFT/GRPO experiments, training-data ablations, and real-world benchmark results in Tables 1–3, alongside retained appendix results.

M1.justification: The main training prescription changes from staged GRPO curriculum learning with an Answer-Equivalence BERT cosine-similarity reward to mixed-data training with an average ROUGE-1/2/L reward. This substantively changes the learning procedure and reward signal. The earlier curriculum plots nevertheless remain in Appendix E.

E1.justification: v4 adds actual evaluation on MVBench and MMVU, extending assessment to real-world temporal and multidisciplinary video understanding. Its main training study replaces the explicitly physics-focused PhysBench stage with general video QA from Video-R1/LLaVA-Video. VideoHallu's seven generators, four categories, and total dataset size remain unchanged.

E2.justification: v4 adds LLaVA-OneVision and matched SFT comparators for Qwen2.5-VL-7B and LLaVA-OneVision. The main leaderboard replaces GPT-4o with GPT-4o-mini and Gemini-2.5-Flash with Gemini-2.0-Flash. The fine-tuning table also changes its previous-model comparator set, although older comparisons survive in the appendices.

E3.justification: The reported split changes from 800 training/2,433 testing pairs to 800 training/908 validation/1,525 testing pairs, and the answer judge changes from GPT-4 to GPT-4o-mini. The new SFT/GRPO study uses 2,000 real plus 800 synthetic examples across two architectures. The main R1 comparison is now described as CoT-prompted rather than separately reporting direct-answer and CoT conditions.

E4.justification: v4 adds SFT-versus-GRPO analyses across two architectures and explicitly tests whether synthetic training harms real-world performance. Its main data ablations compare real-only, synthetic-only, and mixed training, replacing the earlier emphasis on general-versus-physics curricula. The old curriculum charts, question-type breakdown, and appendix hallucination cases are retained, not newly added analyses.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Both audit the answer judge using 200 randomly sampled answer pairs; the changed agreement percentage is a result change, not a change in uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: The main leaderboard changes from Qwen2.5-VL-32B leading at 51.4% to Video-R1 leading at 53.64%, under different splits and judges. New v4 results include Qwen SFT/GRPO accuracies of 51.02%/57.69% and combined-training MMVU/MVBench scores of 61.3/70.1. These are revised or newly reported results, not same-setting gains over v3. The earlier question-type scores remain unchanged in v4 Table 7.

T1.justification: v4 adds formal SFT and preference-pair training objectives in Equations 1–2 and changes the mathematical reward definition. The benchmark's contextual-distance objective and constraints are retained in Appendix B with renumbering and notation edits. No new theorem or proof is introduced.

C1.justification: v4 reframes VideoHallu as negative-control testing of genuine visual understanding and introduces the claim that synthetic-data GRPO improves this ability without degrading standard benchmark performance. This replaces the contribution centered on a physics curriculum and roughly 3% synthetic-benchmark improvement, while retaining the central hallucination finding.

C2.justification: v4 interprets GRPO's advantage over SFT as transferable reasoning versus surface-pattern memorization, argues that real data stabilizes synthetic-data training, and discusses coexistence of real and synthetic video abilities. It also newly compares benchmark performance with a 50% random baseline. The annotation-cost and scalability limitations remain substantially unchanged.

D1.justification: v4 documents 15 training frames, a 1e-6 learning rate, Open-R1, eight A100 80GB GPUs, video metadata, and the judge prompt. The one-epoch budget remains, while v3's gradient-accumulation disclosure disappears. The release statement changes from code availability to data availability at the same repository. These disclosures do not establish changes to previously unspecified settings.

R1.justification: The related-work positioning shifts from video-generation scoring and general video understanding toward RL post-training and synthetic-content monitoring. v4 adds discussions and citations including Vision-R1, R1-VL, More Thinking, Less Seeing?, and Bi-LoRA, while removing much of the earlier VideoScore/VBench-centered coverage. This substantially revises the research context.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, training section, and much of related work are extensively rewritten. Terminology shifts from MLLMs to VLMs, the benchmark formulation moves into Appendix B, and the appendices are reorganized around examples, formulation, categorization, prompts, charts, and question-type analysis.

P2.justification: Figure 1 replaces its score-based evaluation panel with a positive-control example; the categorization and main case-study figures are redrawn. Main result tables change from thirteen subcategories to four category columns, the taxonomy table disappears, and a real-world results table is added. The unchanged radar charts move into Appendix E.

improvement.justification: v4 adds useful SFT/GRPO comparisons, real-world retention tests, and implementation details. However, its discussion still says all R1 models underperform the base despite Table 1 showing Video-R1 at 53.64% versus 52.98%; Appendices E–F retain earlier experiments and scores without reconciling the changed protocol. The new preference-pair objective is also not connected clearly to the reported ROUGE-reward training. These benefits and unresolved consistency problems prevent a reliable net quality judgment.
